**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, sitting at the kitchen table with a math worksheet smeared with eraser dust. The numbers blurred together, and my fingers ached from gripping the pencil too tight. His voice wasn’t loud—it didn’t need to be. The words settled in my chest like a stone dropped into a well, and I’ve been carrying them ever since.

Words are supposed to be light, aren’t they? Just air pushed through vocal cords, shapes on a page. But some stick. Some burrow. Some become part of the skeleton.

II.

I once read that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. That’s 16,000 chances to build or destroy, to connect or sever, to lie or tell the truth. Most of them are forgettable—*"Pass the salt," "What time is it?"*—but some linger like ghosts. The *"I love you"* whispered in the dark. The *"It’s over"* that cracks the world in half.

I think about the words I’ve swallowed. The *"I’m scared"* I didn’t say before my first job interview. The *"I miss you"* I texted and then deleted. The *"Help me"* that got stuck in my throat like a fishbone. What do those unsaid words weigh? Do they rot inside us, or do they just… dissolve?

III.

There’s a myth—maybe it’s true—that every word ever spoken still exists somewhere, vibrating in the fabric of the universe. That means my first stuttering *"Mama"* is still out there, floating beside Hitler’s speeches, beside Martin Luther King’s *"I have a dream,"* beside the last words of someone who died alone in a hospital bed. All of it, endless, overlapping, a cacophony of human noise.

If that’s true, then silence must be the only real absence. The spaces between words are where we hide the things we can’t name.

IV.

I had a professor in college who said, *"Language is a prison."* At the time, I thought he was being dramatic. But now I understand. How do you explain grief? How do you describe the color of the sky at the exact moment the sun sets? How do you tell someone you love them without it sounding like a cliché or a demand or a lie?

We’re all just pointing at things and hoping the other person sees the same shadow.

V.

I keep a journal. Not the kind with lock and key, but a plain black notebook where I write things I’m afraid to say out loud. Some pages are filled with rage—screams at people who will never read them. Some are love letters to versions of myself I’ve outgrown. Some are just lists: *Things That Make Me Want to Disappear*, *Reasons to Stay*, *Names I’ve Been Called*.

Writing them down makes them feel less like a storm inside me and more like… weather. Something that passes.

VI.

The heaviest word I know is *"why."*

Why did she leave? Why him and not me? Why does the world keep spinning when everything hurts? It’s a word that demands an answer, but the answer is always another question, a hall of mirrors with no exit.

The lightest word is *"yes."* Or maybe *"okay."* Words that don’t ask for anything. Words that let you float for a moment before gravity remembers you.

VII.

I had a dream once where I was standing in a library, but the books were made of flesh. When I opened one, the pages bled. The librarian told me, *"Every story costs something."* I woke up with my heart pounding and the taste of iron in my mouth.

VIII.

Here’s what I believe: Words are spells. The right ones can heal; the wrong ones can curse. *"You’re beautiful"* can mend a broken day. *"You’ll never amount to anything"* can haunt a lifetime.

We should handle them like live wires.

IX.

I’m running out of words now. Or maybe I’ve just run out of things to say. The cursor blinks at me, impatient. *Fill me, it seems to demand. Make me mean something.*

But what if the most honest thing is the silence after the last word? The breath before the next thought? The space where we stop performing and just… are?

X.

I started with a memory of my father. I’ll end with one of my mother.

She used to hum while she cooked, old songs she didn’t know the words to. One evening, I asked her why she never sang the lyrics. She looked at me, stirring a pot of soup, and said, *"Some things are better felt than said."*

Then she handed me a spoon. *"Taste this,"* she told me. *"Tell me if it needs salt."*

And for once, I didn’t have to search for the right words. I just nodded and said, *"Perfect."*
